blocks.text: But what, you will say, does the swallow have in common with birds of prey, that it should take its name from seizing? To me it makes no difference: whatever the reason it is so called, it is nevertheless certain that it is so called. But the origin of the name is also clear enough, since the swallow is carnivorous and lives only by seizing prey. Hence Isidore, Origins, book 12, chapter 7: The swallow is so called because it does not take its food sitting, but SEIZES its food in the air and eats it. And the Philosopher more than once calls it σαρκοφάγον [sarkophagon]. Thus in History of Animals, book 6, chapter 5: Ἡ δὲ χελιδὼν δὶς νεοττεύει μόνον [II, 836] τῶν σαρκοφάγων [Hē de chelidōn dis neotteuei monon tōn sarkophagōn]; The swallow alone of carnivorous animals nests twice. And in book 8, chapter 3: Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ τῶν μὴ γαμψωνύχων ἔνιοι σαρκοφάγοι, οἷον ἡ χελιδών [Eisi de kai tōn mē gampsōnychōn enioi sarkophagoi, hoion hē chelidōn]. Pliny rendered this in book 10, chapter 24: The swallow is the only bird that feeds on flesh, among those which do not have hooked talons. And Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 8, Problem 7, comparing these two symbols of Pythagoras, Χελιδόνας οἰκίᾳ μὴ δέχεσθαι, μηδὲ γαμψωνύχων οἴκοι τρέφειν [Chelidonas oikia mē dechesthai, mēde gampsōnychōn oikoi trephein], Swallows are not to be admitted into the house, nor birds with hooked talons to be reared in the home, asserts that they rest on the same reason: Σαρκοφάγος γάρ ἐστι (ἡ χελιδὼν) καὶ μάλιστα τοὺς τέττιγας ἱεροὺς καὶ μουσικοὺς ὄντας ἀποκτίννυσι, καὶ σιτεῖται [Sarkophagos gar esti (hē chelidōn) kai malista tous tettigas hierous kai mousikous ontas apoktinnysi, kai siteitai]; For the swallow is carnivorous, he says, and above all kills and devours cicadas, which are sacred and musical. Moreover, Pliny observes of the swallow, in the place cited above, that the speed of its winding flight is so swift that for this reason it is not exposed to the attacks of other birds. Perhaps those who named it from seizing had this in view. For it is well known that in almost all languages verbs of seizing also refer to speed. Thus in Hebrew Kimchi and Mardochaeus explain חטיפה, seizure, as לקיחה במהירות, a snatching with speed. And the Talmudists in Moed [col. 237] Katan ch. 3, fol. 28a: מת פתאום זו היא מיתא חטופא, If someone dies suddenly, this is a snatched death, that is, headlong and swift. Like that saying of Plutarch in the Consolation to Apollonius: Ἐὰν δὲ ταχέως ἀποθάνῃ, ὀδύρονται λέγοντες, Ἀνηρπάσθη [Ean de tacheōs apothanē, odyrontai legontes, Anērpasthē]. If he dies suddenly, they lament, saying, He has been snatched away. Thus you will see ἁρπάγδην [harpagdēn], ἁρπακτικῶς [harpaktikōs], ἁρπαλέως [harpaleōs], ἁρπαλιμῶς [harpalimōs], and, with Kappa prefixed, καρπαλιμῶς [karpalimōs] used everywhere not of plunder but of speed, like Latin rapide [rapidly] and raptim [hurriedly]. Hesychius: Καρπάλιμον· ταχύ [Karpalimon: tachy]. Likewise: Ἁρπυία· ἁρπαγὴ, ἢ διὰ τάχους [Harpyia: harpagē, ē dia tachous]. The Etymologicum: Ἅρπασος· ποταμὸς Καρίας, διὰ τὸ ὀξύτατον τοῦ ῥοῦ [Harpasos: potamos Karias, dia to oxytaton tou rhou]. Virgil, Aeneid book 5:
— — — and suddenly, at the signal heard, they seize the course. — —
Where corripiunt [they seize], says Servius, means they go hurriedly. Persius, Satire 5:
— — nothing prevents you from seizing the Aegean with a huge ship. — — —
Which Casaubon explains as you swiftly cleave. Lucan, book 5, line 403:

Thence he seizes his course, and the fields which the sluggish Apulian has abandoned by the rake and given over to idle grass, swifter than the flames of heaven and the tigress with young, he runs across. — — —
And a little later, [II, 837] It seemed shameful to the leader, at a time for seizing war, to be stuck in sluggish delays. — —
— — — and with seized (rushing) flood the Apidanus, and the Enipeus, never swift unless mingled.
Pliny in the Panegyric: When you led the legions, or rather (so great was your speed) swept them along. A twin to which is that line of Lucan, the poet, on Caesar, book 1:
Use, I warn you, the rushing post-horse more sparingly.

Accordingly Damir, in the chapter On the horse, derives the Arabic name of the horse, فرس [faras] pharas, from seizing, thus: لفظها مشتق من الافتراس كانها تفرس الارض بسرعة مشيتها [lafẓuhā mushtaqq min al-iftirās kaʾannahā tafrisu al-arḍ bi-surʿat mishyatihā] Its name is derived from seizing, as though it tore up the earth by the speed of its gait. And the verb خطف [khaṭafa] chatapha signifies first to seize, then to be swift. From this, then, the swallow could be called خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, as among camels the dromedary is called خيطف [khayṭaf] chaitaph, and a headlong gait حيطفي [ḥayṭafī] chaitapha, and lightning خاطف [khāṭif] chatiph, because it dazzles the eyes, they say, by the rapidity of its motion. Therefore those who take خطاف chottaph, or, what is the same, חטפיתא chatphitha and חטופיתא chatophitha, for a bird of prey of the class τῶν γαμψωνύχων [tōn gampsōnychōn] are as mistaken as those who so take תחמס, since חטפיתא means the swallow, and תחמס the ostrich, as we have tried to prove. Next will follow the exposition of the words with which the ostrich is described in Job: words that are excellent, but, as we think, not yet sufficiently understood, and therefore to be explained here.
